docs.title: Introduction to i18n
docs.text:
🌍 Internationalization (i18n) is the process of designing and developing software applications to support multiple languages and regional preferences. The term "i18n" comes from the first and last letters of "internationalization" and the 18 letters in between.

Key benefits of i18n:

  • 🌐 Expand your user base to global audiences
  • 🤝 Improve user experience by providing content in their preferred language
  • 🚀 Enhance application accessibility
  • 📈 Increase user engagement and satisfaction

Our implementation in this FastAPI project provides a robust framework for translating application text into multiple languages based on user preferences detected from HTTP requests.

docs.title: Implementation Overview
docs.text:
This project implements i18n using Python's built-in gettext module, which is a standard approach for internationalization. The implementation follows these key principles:

  • Singleton Pattern: A TranslationWrapper class that ensures consistent translation behavior throughout the application
  • Middleware-based: Language detection and setting via FastAPI middleware
  • Multiple Detection Methods: Language preferences are detected from query parameters, cookies, or HTTP headers
  • Variable Interpolation: Support for dynamic content within translated strings

docs.title: Project Structure
docs.text:
The i18n implementation consists of the following components:

project/
├── core/
│   └── i18n/
│       ├── base.py         # Core translation functions
│       └── language.py     # Middleware for language detection
├── translations/
│   ├── fa/                 # Persian language
│   │   └── LC_MESSAGES/
│   │       ├── messages.mo # Compiled translation file
│   │       └── messages.po # Human-readable translation file
│   └── messages.pot        # Template file with all translatable strings
└── babel.cfg               # Configuration for Babel extraction

docs.title: Translation Flow
docs.text:
graph TD
    A[Client Request] -->|Headers/Cookies/Query Params| B[LanguageMiddleware]
    B -->|Extracts Language Preference| C[set_locale]
    C -->|Updates Translation Instance| D[TranslationWrapper]
    D -->|Stores Active Translation| E[Application Code]
    E -->|Calls translate| F[gettext]
    F -->|Returns Translated String| G[Response]

When a user sends a request to your FastAPI application, the following process occurs:

  1. 📥 Request Received: The client makes a request to your API
  2. 🔍 Language Detection: The LanguageMiddleware intercepts the request
  3. 🌐 Locale Setting: The set_locale function determines the preferred language from:
  4. ?lang= query parameter (highest priority)
  5. Accept-Language cookie (medium priority)
  6. Accept-Language HTTP header (lowest priority)
  7. 🔄 Translation Setup: The TranslationWrapper singleton is updated with the correct language
  8. 💬 String Translation: Application code calls translate() or _() functions with message strings
  9. 📤 Response Delivery: Translated content is included in the response

docs.title: Setup and Configuration
docs.text:
To set up i18n in your FastAPI project:

  1. Install Required Dependencies: 

    uv add babel

  2. Create a Babel Configuration File (babel.cfg): 

    [python: **.py]
encoding = utf-8

  3. Add Middleware to Your FastAPI App: 

    from core.i18n.language import LanguageMiddleware

app = FastAPI()
app.add_middleware(LanguageMiddleware)

  4. Initialize Translation Directory: 

    mkdir -p translations
uv run pybabel extract -F babel.cfg -o translations/messages.pot .

  5. Create the .po Files for the Languages You Want to Support: 

    uv run pybabel init -i translations/messages.pot -d translations -l fa
uv run pybabel init -i translations/messages.pot -d translations -l de

  6. Compile the .po Files Into .mo Files: 

    uv run pybabel compile -d translations

docs.title: Basic Translation
docs.text:
To translate a string in your application:

from core.i18n.base import translate

# Option 1: Using the translate function
translated_text = translate("Hello, world!")

# Option 2: Using the shorthand _ function (if installed)
from core.i18n.base import translate as _
translated_text = _("Hello, world!")

docs.title: Real-world Example from Your Code:
docs.text:
async def register_user(self, *, register_user_request: RegisterUserRequest) -> UserResponse:
    user = await self.user_repository.get_by_email(email=register_user_request.email)
    if user:
        raise BadRequestException(message=_("User already exists with this email."))

    # Rest of the function...

In this example, the error message is translated based on the user's language preference.

docs.title: Translation with Variables
docs.text:
For dynamic content, use the translate_with_variables function:

from core.i18n.base import translate_with_variables

# Example with variables
username = "Alice"
count = 5
message = translate_with_variables(
    "Hello, {username}! You have {count} new messages.",
    username=username,
    count=count
)

docs.title: Example from Your Code:
docs.text:
@user_router.get("test/")
async def test():
    a = 20
    b = "test str"

    # Use translate_with_variables to handle dynamic placeholders
    return {"message": translate_with_variables("a equals {a} and b equals {b}", a=a, b=b)}

When this endpoint is called:

  • With English as the preferred language: "a equals 20 and b equals test str"
  • With Persian as the preferred language (assuming translation exists): "a برابر است با 20 و b برابر است با test str"

docs.title: How Variable Translation Works:
docs.text:
1. The base message is extracted and appears in the messages.pot file: 

    #: app/api/test.py:10
msgid "a equals {a} and b equals {b}"
msgstr ""

  2. Translators provide translations while preserving the placeholders: 

    # German example
msgid "a equals {a} and b equals {b}"
msgstr "a برابر است با 20 و b برابر است با test str"

  3. At runtime, the placeholders are replaced with the actual values.

Warning

Placeholders must be preserved exactly as they appear in the original string. The position can change to match the grammar of the target language, but the names must remain the same.

docs.title: Understanding Translation Files
docs.text:
The i18n workflow uses three types of files:

  1. POT (Portable Object Template) Files (.pot):
  2. Template files containing all extractable strings from your code
  3. Generated by scanning the source code for translatable strings

  4. Acts as a starting point for creating translations

  5. PO (Portable Object) Files (.po):

  6. Human-readable files containing source strings and their translations
  7. One file per language

  8. Edited by translators to provide translations for each string

  9. MO (Machine Object) Files (.mo):

  10. Binary, compiled versions of PO files
  11. Used at runtime by the application
  12. Generated from PO files using the pybabel compile command

docs.title: Adding New Translations
docs.text:
When adding new translatable strings to your application, follow this workflow to preserve existing translations:

  1. Extract New Messages: 

    uv run pybabel extract -F babel.cfg -o translations/messages.pot .

  2. Update Existing PO Files: 

    uv run pybabel update -i translations/messages.pot -d translations
    This merges new messages into existing PO files without overwriting existing translations.

  3. Edit Translations:

    Open the .po files (e.g., translations/fa/LC_MESSAGES/messages.po)

    Add translations for the new messages

  4. Compile Updated Translations: 

    uv run pybabel compile -d translations

docs.title: Setting Up Translations in a New Environment
docs.text:
When a developer pulls the project from a repository, they need to regenerate the .mo files since these are typically excluded from version control (in .gitignore). Here's the process:

  1. Clone the Repository: 

    git clone <repository-url>
cd <project-directory>

  2. Install Dependencies: 

    uv sync

  3. Extract New Messages: 

    uv run pybabel extract -F babel.cfg -o translations/messages.pot .

  4. Compile Translation Files: 

    uv run pybabel compile -d translations

Tip

💡 The .po files should be committed to the repository, while .mo files are compiled locally.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• 🔄 Use variables wisely: For complex sentences with multiple variables, consider breaking them into smaller, more manageable strings.
  • 🌐 Test with RTL languages: If supporting languages like Arabic or Persian, ensure your UI handles right-to-left text correctly.
  • 📝 Add context for translators: Use comments in your code to provide context for translators: 
    # Translators: This appears on the login page
error_message = _("Invalid username or password")
  • 🔍 Keep translations consistent: Maintain a glossary of common terms to ensure consistency across translations.
  • 🤝 Consider pluralization: For messages involving counts, use gettext's plural forms support.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Issue Potential Solution Translations not appearing Ensure .mo files are compiled and in the correct location New strings not extracted Check your babel.cfg configuration Wrong language detected Debug the language detection logic in set_locale Placeholder errors Ensure all placeholders in translations match the original string

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This project uses Alembic, a database migration tool for SQLAlchemy, to manage database schema changes in a controlled and versioned manner. Migrations allow you to evolve your database schema over time while preserving existing data.

Key benefits of using Alembic:

  • Track database schema changes in version control
  • Easily upgrade or downgrade your database to specific versions
  • Automatically generate migration scripts based on model changes
  • Apply migrations consistently across different environments

docs.title: Directory Structure
docs.text:
migrations/
├── env.py                # Environment configuration for Alembic
├── README                # Documentation
├── script.py.mako        # Template for generating migration scripts
└── versions/             # Directory containing all migration versions
    ├── 2025_01_16_0414_17f9dafacfb9_add_user_table.py
    └── 2025_01_18_0629_3f15bec04ed2_add_posts_table.py

docs.title: alembic.ini
docs.text:
This is the main configuration file for Alembic. Key settings include:

  • script_location: Path to migration scripts (migrations)
  • file_template: Format for naming migration files (customized to include date and time)
  • version_path_separator: Used when specifying multiple version paths
  • Logging configuration settings

docs.title: env.py
docs.text:
This script configures how Alembic interacts with your application:

  • Connects Alembic to your SQLAlchemy models (Base.metadata)
  • Configures database connection settings from your application config
  • Defines migration execution methods for both online and offline modes
  • Sets up proper Python path to access your application modules

docs.title: Migration Naming Convention
docs.text:
Our migrations follow this naming pattern: 

YYYY_MM_DD_HHMM_<revision_id>_<slug>.py

For example: 

2025_01_16_0414_17f9dafacfb9_add_user_table.py

Where:

  • 2025_01_16: Year, month, day (January 16, 2025)
  • 0414: Time (4:14 AM)
  • 17f9dafacfb9: Unique revision ID generated by Alembic
  • add_user_table: Descriptive slug describing the migration's purpose

This naming convention allows for:

  • Easy chronological sorting of migrations
  • Quick identification of when a migration was created
  • Clear understanding of what each migration does

docs.title: Creating a New Migration
docs.text:
To generate a new migration script:

make generate-migration

You'll be prompted to enter a migration message (e.g., "add_user_profile_fields"). This command runs alembic revision --autogenerate -m "your_message", which:

  1. Examines the differences between your current models and database
  2. Creates a new migration script in the versions/ directory
  3. Adds both upgrade() and downgrade() functions to the script
Tip

Always review auto-generated migrations before applying them. Alembic may not detect all changes correctly (especially complex ones like renamed columns).

Example migration script:

2025_01_18_0629_3f15bec04ed2_add_posts_table.py
def upgrade():
    # Add new posts table
    op.create_table(
        'posts',
        sa.Column('id', sa.Integer(), nullable=False),
        sa.Column('title', sa.String(length=100), nullable=False),
        sa.Column('content', sa.Text(), nullable=True),
        sa.Column('user_id', sa.Integer(), nullable=False),
        sa.ForeignKeyConstraint(['user_id'], ['users.id']),
        sa.PrimaryKeyConstraint('id')
    )

def downgrade():
    # Drop the posts table
    op.drop_table('posts')

docs.title: Applying Migrations
docs.text:
To apply all pending migrations up to the latest version:

make migrate

This runs alembic upgrade head, which:

  • Identifies which migrations haven't been applied
  • Runs each migration's upgrade() function in the correct order
  • Updates Alembic's version tracking table in your database

docs.title: Rolling Back Migrations
docs.text:
To roll back the most recent migration:

make rollback

This executes alembic downgrade -1, which:

  • Runs the downgrade() function of the most recent migration
  • Updates Alembic's version tracking to reflect the change

docs.title: Complete Database Reset
docs.text:
To roll back all migrations and start fresh:

make reset-database

This runs alembic downgrade base, which:

  • Sequentially executes all downgrade() functions in reverse order
  • Returns the database to its initial state before any migrations were applied

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Descriptive migration names 📝

  2. Use clear, concise descriptions in migration messages

  3. Example: "add_user_table" instead of "update1"

  4. Test migrations before deployment 🧪

  5. Verify both upgrade() and downgrade() functions work correctly

  6. Test on a copy of production data when possible

  7. One logical change per migration 🧩

  8. Keep migrations focused on a single purpose

  9. Easier to understand, test, and troubleshoot

  10. Include both up and down migrations ⬆️⬇️

  11. Always implement the downgrade() function

  12. Ensures you can roll back changes if needed

  13. Data migrations 📊

  14. When changing column types or structure, don't forget to migrate existing data

  15. May require custom SQL or Python code in migrations

  16. Review auto-generated migrations 👀

  17. Auto-generation is convenient but not perfect

  18. Always check for correctness before applying

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text: Command Description alembic init migrations Initialize a new Alembic environment alembic revision --autogenerate -m "message" Generate a new migration automatically alembic revision -m "message" Create a blank migration manually alembic upgrade head Apply all pending migrations alembic upgrade +1 Apply the next pending migration alembic downgrade -1 Roll back the most recent migration alembic downgrade base Roll back all migrations alembic current Show current migration version alembic history Show migration history

docs.title: Missing Tables
docs.text:
If Alembic complains about missing tables when generating migrations:

  • Ensure your models are properly imported in env.py
  • Verify that target_metadata is correctly set to your Base.metadata

docs.title: Autogenerate Not Detecting Changes
docs.text:
Alembic might not detect certain changes:

  • Constraints and indexes may need manual specification
  • Changes to server defaults might not be detected
  • Custom column types might require special handling

docs.title: Migration Order Conflicts
docs.text:
If you encounter order conflicts:

  • Use alembic merge to combine conflicting migrations
  • Consider using branches for complex concurrent development

docs.title: Custom API Response
docs.text:
🚀 Clean, Consistent API Responses with Standardized Structure

Our FastAPI application implements a custom response system that wraps all API responses in a standardized format. This approach provides several benefits:

  • Consistency: All endpoints return responses with the same structure
  • Error handling: Simplified error handling with consistent status reporting
  • Internationalization: Built-in support for translated messages
  • Metadata: Every response includes status information alongside the actual content

docs.title: Response Structure
docs.text:
Each API response follows this JSON structure:

{
  "header": {
    "status": "success|failure",
    "message": "Human-readable message about the operation",
    "code": 200
  },
  "content": {
    // The actual data returned by the endpoint (if any)
  }
}

docs.title: 1. ResponseStatus Enum
docs.text:
class ResponseStatus(StrEnum):
    SUCCESS = auto()
    FAILURE = auto()

This enum defines the possible status values for API responses, automatically converted to lowercase strings in the JSON output ("success" or "failure").

docs.title: 2. APIResponseHeader Model
docs.text:
class APIResponseHeader(BaseModel):
    """Header type for API responses."""
    status: ResponseStatus = Field(default=ResponseStatus.SUCCESS)
    message: str = Field(default=_("Operation completed successfully."))
    code: int = Field(default=HTTPStatus.OK)

The header model encapsulates:

  • status: The operation result (success or failure)
  • message: A human-readable message (with i18n support via the _() translation function)
  • code: The HTTP status code for the response

docs.title: 3. APIResponseType Generic Model
docs.text:
class APIResponseType(BaseModel, Generic[T]):
    """Type definition for API responses."""
    header: APIResponseHeader
    content: Optional[T] = None

This generic model defines the structure of all API responses with:

  • header: Metadata about the response (status, message, code)
  • content: The actual data payload, which can be of any type T or None

docs.title: 4. APIResponse Implementation
docs.text:
class APIResponse(APIResponseType[T], Generic[T]):
    """
    Generic API response wrapper with automatic exception handling.
    """
    def __init__(self, data: T):
        super().__init__(
            header=APIResponseHeader(
                status=ResponseStatus.SUCCESS,
                message=_("Operation completed successfully."),
                code=HTTPStatus.OK,
            ),
            content=data,
        )

This is the concrete implementation that wraps any data in the standardized response format, with default values for successful operations.

docs.title: Example Endpoint
docs.text:
@user_router.get("/{user_id}", dependencies=[Depends(PermissionDependency([IsAuthenticated]))])
@Cache.cached(prefix=prefix, ttl=60)
async def get_user(
    user_id: UUID4,
    user_controller: UserController = Depends(Factory().get_user_controller),
    assert_access: Callable = Depends(Permissions(UserPermission.READ)),
) -> APIResponseType[UserResponse]:
    """
    Get details of a specific user by ID.
    - **path parameter**: `user_id` (UUID)
    - **permissions required**: Authenticated + `user:read`
    - **response**: User object
    """
    user = await user_controller.get_user(uuid=user_id)
    assert_access(resource=user)
    return APIResponse(user)

In this example:

  1. The endpoint declares its return type as APIResponseType[UserResponse]
  2. The business logic retrieves the user data
  3. The raw user object is wrapped in APIResponse(user) before being returned
  4. FastAPI automatically serializes this to the standardized JSON format

docs.title: Example Response
docs.text:
{
  "header": {
    "status": "success",
    "message": "Operation completed successfully.",
    "code": 200
  },
  "content": {
    "uuid": "a3b8f042-1e16-4f0a-a8f0-421e16df0a2f",
    "email": "johndoe@example.com",
    "first_name": "john",
    "last_name": "doe",
    "role": "USER",
    "activated": true
  }
}

docs.title: Consistency
docs.text: All API endpoints return data in the same format, making integration simpler for frontend developers and API consumers.

docs.title: Internationalization
docs.text: Response messages are run through the translation system, allowing for localized error and success messages.

docs.title: Type Safety
docs.text: Thanks to Python's typing system and Pydantic, we get full type checking for our response data.

docs.title: Separation of Concerns
docs.text: The response header (metadata) is clearly separated from the actual content, making it easy to process status information independently from the data.

docs.title: Extensibility
docs.text: The system can be easily extended to include additional metadata in the header or to handle different response scenarios.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always use the APIResponse wrapper: Never return raw data directly from endpoint functions
  2. Define specific return types: Always specify the content type like APIResponseType[UserResponse]
  3. Custom error responses: For error cases, you can create a similar error response class
  4. Keep the pattern consistent: All endpoints should follow this pattern to maintain API consistency

docs.title: Advanced Usage
docs.text:
For handling error scenarios, you might create a companion error response class:

class APIErrorResponse(APIResponseType[None]):
    def __init__(self, message: str, code: int = HTTPStatus.BAD_REQUEST):
        super().__init__(
            header=APIResponseHeader(
                status=ResponseStatus.FAILURE,
                message=message,
                code=code,
            ),
            content=None,
        )

This could be used in exception handlers or directly in endpoints for known error conditions.

✨ By implementing this standardized response system, our API becomes more maintainable, consistent, and developer-friendly while enabling robust client-side error handling.
